reference.source: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
clinicalPearls: Roughly half of cases arise in neurofibromatosis type 1, typically from malignant transformation of a pre-existing plexiform neurofibroma; the remainder are sporadic or radiation-associated.
A rapidly enlarging, newly painful mass in a known NF1 plexiform neurofibroma is the classic warning of transformation and warrants urgent imaging and biopsy.
FDG PET-CT is valuable for distinguishing malignant transformation from a benign neurofibroma and for directing biopsy to the most metabolically active focus.
Loss of nuclear H3K27me3 on immunohistochemistry, reflecting PRC2 (SUZ12/EED) inactivation, is a useful diagnostic adjunct, though not entirely specific.
S100 and SOX10 staining is typically patchy or lost, unlike the diffuse positivity seen in benign nerve sheath tumours.
Wide surgical resection with negative margins is the cornerstone of treatment; the tumour is relatively resistant to radiotherapy and chemotherapy.
Radiation-associated tumours may arise years to decades after therapeutic irradiation and carry a particularly poor outcome.
The lung is the dominant site of distant metastasis, so staging chest imaging is mandatory.
reference.pathophysiology: The tumour originates from Schwann cell or perineurial lineage of the peripheral nerve. In neurofibromatosis type 1, biallelic loss of the NF1 tumour suppressor drives dysregulated RAS-MAPK signalling within a plexiform neurofibroma, and stepwise acquisition of further hits, notably inactivation of CDKN2A and of the polycomb repressive complex 2 components SUZ12 or EED, precipitates high-grade transformation. Loss of PRC2 function causes global loss of the repressive histone mark H3K27me3, promoting aberrant transcription and a spindle-cell sarcoma with fascicular architecture, nuclear pleomorphism and brisk mitotic activity. Sporadic and post-irradiation tumours converge on similar molecular pathways without a germline NF1 defect.
additionalInvestigations: contrast-enhanced MRI of the primary site to assess nerve of origin and local extent
FDG PET-CT to identify malignant transformation and guide biopsy
image-guided core or open incisional biopsy of the most active focus
immunohistochemistry including S100, SOX10 and H3K27me3
staging CT of the thorax for pulmonary metastases
molecular assessment for NF1, CDKN2A and PRC2 alterations
clinical and genetic assessment for underlying neurofibromatosis type 1
redFlags: rapid enlargement of a previously stable neurofibroma
new persistent or nocturnal pain within a known nerve sheath lesion
progressive neurological deficit referable to the involved nerve
hard, fixed mass with rapid growth over weeks
reference.prognosis: Outcome is guarded, with high rates of local recurrence and distant metastasis and a substantial risk of death; large size, high grade, truncal location, incomplete resection and an NF1 background all worsen survival.
pitfalls: mistaking malignant transformation for a benign neurofibroma and delaying biopsy
sampling error from a non-representative biopsy of a heterogeneous mass
assuming radiotherapy or chemotherapy will substitute for inadequate surgical margins
overlooking a second occult tumour or NF1 diagnosis in a young patient
interpreting H3K27me3 loss in isolation as definitive without correlating morphology
references: WHO Classification of Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
Enzinger and Weiss's Soft Tissue Tumors
ESMO Clinical Practice Guidelines for soft tissue sarcoma
management: Wide en-bloc surgical excision with histologically negative margins is the cornerstone of treatment, ideally at a specialist sarcoma unit
Adjuvant radiotherapy to improve local control for large, high-grade or marginally resected tumours, despite limited radiosensitivity
Anthracycline- and ifosfamide-based chemotherapy reserved for high-grade, metastatic or unresectable disease given only modest chemosensitivity
Staging computed tomography of the thorax and management of pulmonary metastases, including metastasectomy for oligometastatic disease
Structured post-treatment surveillance with imaging for local recurrence and distant spread
Coordinated care through a multidisciplinary sarcoma team spanning surgery, radiology, pathology and oncology
Assess for neurofibromatosis type 1, with surveillance of plexiform neurofibromas and genetic counselling where a germline NF1 defect is present
